questions.title: Call Option Payoff and Breakeven
questions.prompt: Walk me through how a call option's payoff works at expiration. If I buy a call with a $50 strike for a $4 premium, and the stock settles at $57 at expiration, what's the payoff, what's my profit, and where exactly is breakeven?
questions.code:
Call payoff = max(S - K, 0)
Profit (buyer) = payoff - premium
Breakeven (long call) = K + premium
questions.modelAnswer: A long call's payoff at expiration is max(S - K, 0): if the stock finishes above the strike, the payoff equals the difference; if it finishes at or below the strike, the option expires worthless and the payoff is zero. Profit for the buyer is payoff minus the premium paid, since the premium is a sunk cost paid upfront regardless of outcome. With S=$57 and K=$50, payoff = max(57-50,0) = $7. Subtracting the $4 premium gives a profit of $3. Breakeven for a long call is strike plus premium ($50+$4=$54) — the stock has to rise enough just to recover what was paid for the option before any real profit begins. The $7 payoff splits into $7 of intrinsic value (what the option is worth if exercised right now) and, at expiration, zero time value, since time value has fully decayed by then.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always separate payoff from profit in my head before doing any math — payoff is just what the option is worth at that instant, profit is payoff minus whatever you paid for the right in the first place. Here the option's $7 in the money, so payoff is $7, but you paid $4 for it, so you actually pocket $3. People sometimes assume any in-the-money option is automatically a win, but if the premium you paid was close to or above the payoff, you can be in the money and still underwater. Breakeven is the number I'd quote first in a trading context — $54 here — because that's the level that actually matters for deciding whether the position was worth putting on.
questions.example: S=$57, K=$50, premium=$4. Payoff = max(57-50, 0) = $7. Profit = $7 - $4 = $3. Breakeven = $50 + $4 = $54 — the stock needed to clear $54 just to cover the premium.
commonMistakes: Reporting the payoff ($7) as the profit, forgetting to subtract the premium paid
Thinking any in-the-money option is automatically profitable regardless of what was paid for it
Computing breakeven as just the strike price, ignoring the premium
Mixing up the payoff formula for a put (max(K-S,0)) with the call formula
keyPoints: Call payoff = max(S - K, 0); never negative
Profit = payoff minus the premium paid (for the buyer)
Breakeven for a long call = strike + premium
Intrinsic value is the payoff if exercised now; time value is the remainder of the premium, which decays to zero by expiration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes payoff using max(S-K,0)
Correctly distinguishes payoff from profit and subtracts the premium
Correctly identifies breakeven as strike plus premium
Articulates intrinsic vs. time value clearly

questions.title: Put-Call Parity Intuition
questions.prompt: Explain put-call parity in your own words. What does C - P = S - K·e^(-rT) actually say, and why must it hold for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock?
questions.modelAnswer: Put-call parity says a call minus a put on the same underlying, strike, and expiration must equal the stock price minus the present value of the strike. It's derived by building two portfolios with identical payoffs at expiration regardless of where the stock ends up: Portfolio A (long call plus a risk-free bond that grows to K) and Portfolio B (long put plus long stock). Both portfolios pay off exactly max(S,K) at expiration in every scenario, so by no-arbitrage they must cost the same today, which rearranges to C - P = S - K·e^(-rT). It holds not because of any assumption about how the stock moves, but purely because two things with identical future payoffs must have identical prices today — if they didn't, you could sell the expensive side, buy the cheap side, and lock in a riskless profit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of parity as a sanity check more than a pricing model — it doesn't tell you what the call or put should individually be worth, only that if you know one, you know the other, given the stock price and the discounted strike. If a desk ever quotes a call and a put that violate this relationship, that's not a market view, that's a mispricing, and it gets arbitraged away almost immediately by anyone paying attention. It's also the first thing I'd check if two option prices looked inconsistent with each other before trusting either one.
questions.example: S=$40, K=$40, r=4% continuous, T=0.5 years, call trades at $3.00. Parity says P = C - S + K·e^(-rT) = 3.00 - 40 + 40·e^(-0.02) = 3.00 - 40 + 39.21 = $2.21. If the put is quoted at $2.80 in the market, it's overpriced relative to the call by about $0.59, and an arbitrageur could sell the put, buy the call, short the stock, and lend the proceeds to lock in that gap risk-free.
commonMistakes: Thinking parity only applies when the market is 'wrong' rather than always holding by construction
Forgetting to discount the strike to present value before comparing it to C - P
Applying the formula unmodified to American options, which can be exercised early
Forgetting the formula needs adjustment for a stock that pays dividends
keyPoints: C - P = S - K·e^(-rT) for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock
Derived from two portfolios with identical payoffs: call+bond vs. put+stock
A violation implies a riskless arbitrage, which is why markets keep prices pinned to it
Holds independent of any model of how the stock price moves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the formula correctly
Explains the replicating-portfolio derivation
Explains why a violation implies arbitrage
Notes the European / no-dividend assumption

questions.title: Pricing a Simple Coupon Bond
questions.prompt: Price a 2-year bond with a $1,000 face value, a 5% annual coupon, and a yield to maturity of 7%. Show your work, and explain why the bond prices below face value.
questions.modelAnswer: Each cash flow is discounted at the 7% yield: Year 1 pays a $50 coupon, discounted to $50/1.07 = $46.73. Year 2 pays the final $50 coupon plus the $1,000 face value, i.e. $1,050, discounted to $1,050/1.07^2 = $1,050/1.1449 = $917.37. Summing gives a price of $46.73 + $917.37 = $964.10. The bond prices below its $1,000 face value because its coupon rate (5%) is below the market's required yield (7%) — a buyer paying face value would only earn 5%, so the price has to fall until the bond's total return (coupon income plus price appreciation to face value at maturity) equals 7%.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always work it cash flow by cash flow rather than trying to shortcut it, especially under interview pressure — write down every payment date, discount each one back at the yield, and add them up. The 'why below face value' part is really just: coupon rate below yield means the market is attaching a value to future cash flows that's below what those cash flows deliver on paper, so the price has to give the buyer the rest of their return through capital appreciation to par at maturity.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to add the face value to the final coupon payment in the last period
Discounting every cash flow by the same single period instead of compounding by each year
Confusing the coupon rate with the yield to maturity
Assuming a bond always prices at face value regardless of yield
keyPoints: Bond price = present value of all coupons plus present value of face value
Each cash flow is discounted at the yield to maturity, compounded by its own time period
Coupon rate below yield → price below face value (discount bond)
Coupon rate above yield → price above face value (premium bond)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly discounts each cash flow at the right power of (1+y)
Correctly includes face value in the final period
Arrives at the correct total price (~$964.10)
Explains the discount-to-par intuition

questions.title: Computing a Basic Sharpe Ratio
questions.prompt: A fund has an annualized return of 11%, the risk-free rate is 3%, and the fund's annualized volatility is 16%. Compute its Sharpe ratio. Is that a strong result?
questions.modelAnswer: Sharpe = (0.11 - 0.03) / 0.16 = 0.08 / 0.16 = 0.50. As a rule of thumb, a Sharpe near 1.0 is considered solid for a systematic strategy, above 2.0 is very strong (and worth double-checking for bias), and below 0.5 is considered weak. A Sharpe of exactly 0.50 sits right at that weak/acceptable boundary — it means the fund is being paid relatively little excess return for the volatility it's taking on, and on its own, over a short sample, this single number also carries meaningful estimation uncertainty.
questions.professionalAnswer: 0.5 is the kind of number where I wouldn't call it bad, but I also wouldn't get excited — it's return the fund is earning for its bumpiness, and 0.5 means you're not getting paid all that generously per unit of volatility. Before judging it further I'd want to know the sample length it came from and whether it's net of fees, because a 0.5 computed gross over six months tells you almost nothing, while the same number over ten years net of fees is a much more informative result.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract the risk-free rate before dividing by volatility
Using return and volatility measured over different periods (e.g. monthly return, annual volatility) without converting
Treating any positive Sharpe as automatically 'good' without a rule-of-thumb benchmark
Not asking what sample length or net/gross basis the ratio was computed over
keyPoints: Sharpe = excess return over the risk-free rate, divided by total volatility
A Sharpe near 1.0 is generally considered solid; below 0.5 is weak
A single Sharpe number needs its sample period and net/gross basis stated to be meaningful

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes Sharpe = 0.50
Correctly characterizes 0.50 relative to standard rules of thumb
Notes the need for sample period / gross-vs-net context

questions.title: Spotting a Survivorship-Bias Mistake
questions.prompt: A junior analyst backtests a 'buy the S&P 500' strategy back to 2005 by pulling today's list of S&P 500 constituents and assuming that list applied the whole time. What's wrong with this, and what should they do instead?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a textbook survivorship bias mistake: using today's index membership and applying it retroactively silently excludes every company that was in the S&P 500 at some point since 2005 but has since been delisted, gone bankrupt, or been acquired. Because the companies that disappear from an index are, on average, the worst performers, a backtest built this way systematically overstates the historical return of holding 'the S&P 500' at any given point in the past. The fix is to use a point-in-time universe — a historical record of which companies were actually members of the index on each date being tested — so that the backtest includes the eventual losers and not just the survivors that happen to still be in the index today.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of the first things I check when I'm handed someone else's backtest — ask exactly how the universe was built. If the answer is 'I pulled the current constituent list,' that's an immediate red flag regardless of how good the numbers look, because every stock that got removed for underperforming or going under is just missing from the test. It's an easy mistake to make because current constituent lists are the easy, free data to get, and point-in-time membership data usually costs more or takes more work to source.
commonMistakes: Assuming index membership is static and doesn't change over time
Treating 'current constituents' and 'point-in-time constituents' as interchangeable
Not realizing that acquisitions are a partial exception (often a positive outcome for the acquired company's shareholders) worth separating from outright delistings/bankruptcies
Fixing the universe but still carrying other look-ahead issues, like using restated fundamental data
keyPoints: Survivorship bias excludes historical failures by building the universe from today's survivors
Companies that disappear from an index are disproportionately the underperformers
The fix is point-in-time index membership, not a static current list
This bias always inflates backtested performance, never deflates it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names the problem as survivorship bias
Explains why it inflates (not deflates) backtested returns
Proposes point-in-time universe membership as the fix
Notes the acquisition vs. delisting nuance

questions.title: Why Diversification Reduces Risk
questions.prompt: Explain why combining two imperfectly correlated assets in a portfolio produces less risk than the simple weighted average of their individual risks. What happens as correlation approaches 1, and what happens as it approaches -1?
questions.modelAnswer: A two-asset portfolio's variance has a cross term, 2·w1·w2·ρ·σ1·σ2, in addition to each asset's own weighted variance. As long as correlation ρ is below 1, that cross term is smaller than it would be if the assets moved in lockstep, which makes the combined portfolio's standard deviation come out below the simple weighted average of the two individual standard deviations — that gap is the diversification benefit. As ρ approaches 1, the cross term grows and the benefit shrinks toward zero: two perfectly correlated assets provide no diversification at all, and portfolio volatility becomes exactly the weighted average. As ρ approaches -1, the cross term becomes strongly negative, and it's possible to construct a combination where the two assets' moves offset almost completely, driving portfolio volatility toward a much smaller number — in the limit, a perfectly hedged, nearly risk-free combination.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd explain this to someone without the formula in front of them: risk doesn't just add up when you combine assets, because what matters is how often they move against each other, not just how much each one moves on its own. Two assets that are highly correlated basically behave like one bigger position — you haven't actually spread your risk, you've just made the same bet bigger. The real diversification benefit only shows up when you hold things that genuinely don't move together, and the lower that correlation gets, the more the portfolio's volatility falls below what a naive weighted average would suggest.
questions.example: With σ1=20%, σ2=30%, ρ=0.3, w1=w2=0.5: portfolio volatility comes out to about 20.4%, well below the 25% simple average of 20% and 30% — that 4.6-point gap is pure diversification benefit from the assets not being perfectly correlated.
commonMistakes: Assuming portfolio risk is simply the weighted average of individual asset risks
Forgetting the cross term in the two-asset variance formula entirely
Believing diversification eliminates all risk rather than only unsystematic risk
Confusing covariance (scale-dependent) with correlation (normalized, -1 to +1)
keyPoints: Portfolio variance includes a correlation-dependent cross term, not just weighted individual variances
Lower correlation produces a bigger diversification benefit
At ρ=1, there is no diversification benefit; at ρ=-1, risk can be nearly eliminated
Diversification only reduces unsystematic (asset-specific) risk, not market-wide systematic risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States and explains the two-asset variance formula with its cross term
Correctly describes the ρ→1 case (no benefit)
Correctly describes the ρ→-1 case (risk near-elimination)
Notes the limit (systematic risk remains regardless)

questions.title: Explaining VaR to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A business unit head who isn't quantitative asks you what 'our 1-day 99% VaR is $2 million' actually means. How do you explain it in plain terms without losing accuracy?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain it as: on a typical day, we don't expect to lose anywhere near $2 million, but on roughly 1 out of every 100 trading days, we'd expect a loss that exceeds $2 million — it's a threshold, not a worst case. I'd be explicit that it does not mean $2 million is the most we could ever lose; it means losses bigger than that are supposed to be rare, specifically a 1-in-100-day event, and that the number is only meaningful with both the confidence level (99%) and horizon (1 day) attached, since 'VaR is $2 million' alone, without those two pieces, is an incomplete statement.
questions.professionalAnswer: I try to get across two things in under a minute: it's a threshold, not a ceiling, and it's silent about how bad the bad day actually gets. I'll usually say something like, 'think of it as a weather forecast for a 1-in-100-day storm — it tells you how often we'd expect to see a loss past this line, not how deep the worst flood could get.' If they push further I'll bring up Expected Shortfall as the number that actually answers 'how bad does it get on those bad days,' since that's usually their next question anyway.
commonMistakes: Describing VaR as the maximum possible loss
Omitting the confidence level or time horizon when stating the number
Implying VaR says anything about how severe a loss beyond the threshold would be
Using jargon like 'quantile of the P&L distribution' without translating it
keyPoints: VaR is a threshold not expected to be exceeded with a given confidence, over a given horizon
It is not the worst-case or maximum possible loss
Both the confidence level and horizon must be stated for the number to be meaningful
VaR says nothing about severity beyond the threshold — that's what Expected Shortfall is for

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives an accurate, jargon-free plain-language explanation
Explicitly corrects the 'maximum loss' misconception
Mentions the confidence level and horizon as necessary context
Connects to Expected Shortfall as the natural follow-up

questions.title: Why a Quantitative Analyst Role
questions.prompt: How do you describe the quantitative analyst role, and what distinguishes it from a quant researcher or quant trader role at the same firm?
questions.modelAnswer: A quant analyst sits closer to the business and risk side than a quant researcher or quant trader: the role is about translating market behavior, pricing, and risk into decisions and reports other people act on — things like pricing a position, measuring a portfolio's risk exposures, running performance attribution, or building a stress-testing or valuation framework — rather than originating new trading signals (researcher) or executing and managing live positions in real time (trader). A quant researcher leans heaviest on statistics and model-building to find an edge; a quant trader leans heaviest on market intuition and decisiveness under live conditions; a quant analyst leans on translating quantitative finance into clear, defensible analysis for traders, portfolio managers, and risk committees.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put it this way: the researcher is trying to find the edge, the trader is running it live, and the analyst is making sure everyone understands what the position is actually exposed to and why it's performing the way it is. I'm drawn to that translation layer — I like being able to go deep on the Greeks, the risk model, or the attribution numbers, but ultimately produce something a PM or a risk committee can act on without needing to rebuild my analysis themselves.
commonMistakes: Describing all three roles (researcher, trader, analyst) as interchangeable
Focusing only on technical skills without explaining what the role actually produces day to day
Overclaiming trading-desk decision authority that an analyst role typically doesn't have
Giving a generic 'I like math and markets' answer without specifics
keyPoints: Quant analyst: translates pricing, risk, and performance analysis into decisions for traders/PMs/risk committees
Quant researcher: designs and backtests signals/models, heaviest on statistics
Quant trader: executes and manages live risk, heaviest on market intuition and speed
Role lines blur more at smaller firms than at large ones

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly distinguishes analyst from researcher and trader roles
Gives concrete examples of analyst deliverables (risk reports, attribution, pricing analysis)
Shows genuine, specific motivation rather than a generic answer

questions.title: Why Market Makers Quote Both Sides
questions.prompt: A market maker quotes a stock at $142.10 bid / $142.14 ask. Where does that $0.04 spread actually come from, and why does it widen when the market turns volatile?
questions.modelAnswer: The spread compensates the market maker for three distinct risks: order-processing cost (the operational cost of handling the trade), inventory risk (the risk of holding a position between trades while the price moves against them), and adverse selection (the risk of trading against a counterparty who knows something they don't). In calm, liquid conditions order-processing cost dominates and spreads stay tight. In volatile or uncertain conditions, inventory risk rises (a position held even briefly is more likely to move against the market maker) and adverse selection rises (informed traders are more likely to be active), so the market maker widens the spread to compensate for both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as three separate charges stacked on top of each other, not one undifferentiated fee: a small baseline for just running the operation, a bigger piece for the risk of getting caught holding inventory, and a piece that grows specifically when the market maker suspects they might be trading against someone smarter than them. Volatility hits the second and third pieces directly, which is exactly why spreads blow out right when you'd most want to trade.
commonMistakes: Treating the spread as pure, risk-free profit for the market maker
Forgetting the adverse selection component entirely
Assuming the spread is fixed or set by regulation rather than by the market maker's own risk assessment
Confusing the bid-ask spread with a brokerage commission
keyPoints: Spread = order-processing cost + inventory risk + adverse selection
Inventory risk and adverse selection both rise in volatile or uncertain conditions, widening the spread
Tick size puts a floor under how narrow a spread can get
The spread is compensation for risk, not a free fee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names all three spread components
Explains why volatility widens the spread
Does not mischaracterize the spread as risk-free profit

questions.title: Market Order or Limit Order?
questions.prompt: You need to exit a position in a thinly-traded stock right before the close, and separately you want to buy into a liquid large-cap only if it dips to a specific price. Which order type fits each situation, and what do you give up with each choice?
questions.modelAnswer: For the urgent exit right before the close in a thin name, a market order is appropriate: it guarantees execution (the position is actually closed before the deadline), at the cost of not guaranteeing price — in a thin book, that could mean a worse fill than expected, especially if the order has to walk through multiple price levels. For the opportunistic buy at a specific dip level in a liquid name with no urgency, a limit order is the right tool: it guarantees the price (you'll never pay more than your limit), at the cost of not guaranteeing execution — if the stock never trades down to that level, the order simply sits unfilled.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always ask myself one question first: is price or time the thing I actually can't compromise on here? If I absolutely need to be out of a position by the close, I accept a worse price and use a market order. If I'm patient and only want the trade at my price, I use a limit order and accept that it might never fill. Mixing those up — using a limit order when I actually needed certainty of execution — is the classic beginner mistake.
commonMistakes: Using a market order in a thin book without expecting a possibly poor average fill price
Using a limit order when execution certainty, not price, was actually the priority
Assuming a limit order always fills once the stock trades near the limit price
Forgetting that a limit order resting unfilled still carries opportunity cost
keyPoints: Market order: guarantees execution, not price
Limit order: guarantees price, not execution
The right choice depends on whether urgency or price control matters more in that situation
A thin book increases the risk that a market order fills at a worse average price

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches market order to the urgent-exit scenario
Correctly matches limit order to the price-sensitive scenario
Clearly states the tradeoff given up in each case

questions.title: Who Gets Filled First on the Order Book
questions.prompt: Three resting limit buy orders sit at $50.02 (submitted 9:31am), $50.02 (submitted 9:30am), and $50.03 (submitted 9:35am). A market sell order arrives for a size that can only fill one of them. Which order fills, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The $50.03 order fills first, even though it was submitted last. Exchanges use price-time priority: price always wins first — a more aggressive bid of $50.03 fills ahead of any bid at $50.02, regardless of submission time. Time only acts as a tiebreaker among orders at the identical price, which is why the two $50.02 orders' relative submission times (9:30 vs 9:31) are irrelevant here; neither of them trades at all until the $50.03 order, and any size behind it at $50.02, is exhausted.
questions.professionalAnswer: The instinct to reach for 'first come, first served' is understandable but wrong here — price always wins before time ever gets a say. I'd explain it as: the book sorts by price first, and only breaks ties within the same price level by arrival time. The $50.03 bid is simply a better bid, full stop, and it trades first no matter when it showed up.
commonMistakes: Assuming the earliest-submitted order always fills first regardless of price
Applying time priority before checking price priority
Not recognizing that canceling and re-submitting an order at the same price resets its time priority
Confusing this with how a dark pool or OTC venue might match orders differently
keyPoints: Price priority always comes before time priority
Time priority only breaks ties between orders at the identical price
A more aggressive price always fills ahead of a less aggressive one, regardless of arrival order
Canceling and resubmitting an order resets its time priority at most exchanges

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the $50.03 order as filling first
Correctly explains price priority outranks time priority
Correctly explains time priority's role as a tiebreaker only

questions.title: Designing a VWAP Execution Schedule
questions.prompt: A client needs to sell 500,000 shares of a mid-cap stock over the course of a trading day without excessively moving the price. Why is a single large market order a bad idea here, and how would a VWAP execution approach handle it differently?
questions.modelAnswer: A single market order for 500,000 shares would exhaust the resting liquidity at the best ask and keep walking to progressively worse prices until fully filled, producing significant market impact and slippage — and part of that price move would likely stick permanently, since a large order conveys information that other participants react to. A VWAP (Volume-Weighted Average Price) approach instead breaks the order into many smaller pieces, sizing each piece in proportion to the market's typical trading volume at that time of day — trading more during the naturally busy periods (open, close) when the market can absorb size with less impact, and less during quiet mid-day periods. The goal is to get the whole 500,000 shares filled at a price close to the day's natural volume-weighted average, rather than paying the full cost of walking through the book in one shot.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it to the client as: you're trading off speed against cost, and a single market order chooses 'fastest, most expensive' by default. Spreading the order out using VWAP lets you ride the market's own natural liquidity instead of forcing yourself through it — you trade more when the market can absorb it, less when it can't, and you walk away from the day much closer to what a 'fair' average price looks like.
commonMistakes: Assuming market impact only matters for retail-sized trades
Confusing VWAP (volume-proportional) with TWAP (time-proportional) execution
Ignoring the permanent component of market impact, assuming the price always fully snaps back
Treating VWAP execution as risk-free just because it reduces impact
keyPoints: A single large market order causes both temporary and permanent market impact
VWAP sizes execution slices in proportion to typical volume at each time of day
The goal is a fill price close to the day's volume-weighted average, not the fastest possible fill
Spreading execution out trades off speed for lower expected cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why a single large market order is costly here
Correctly describes how VWAP sizing works
Articulates the speed-vs-cost tradeoff clearly

questions.title: Common Stock vs Preferred Stock
questions.prompt: An investor asks why they'd ever choose preferred stock over common stock in the same company. What's actually different between the two, and what's the tradeoff?
questions.modelAnswer: Common stock carries voting rights and a residual claim on profit — common shareholders get whatever's left after every other obligation is paid, which means unlimited upside but no priority. Preferred stock typically pays a fixed dividend that must be paid before any common dividend, and has priority over common stock if the company is liquidated, but usually carries no voting rights and doesn't share in the company's upside the way common stock does. The tradeoff is priority and stability versus upside and control: preferred sits between common stock and bonds in the risk/return spectrum, trading away growth potential for a more predictable, senior claim.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the investor: preferred is for someone who wants bond-like predictability with slightly more upside than a bond, while common is for someone who wants to actually own a piece of the business's future, including its risk. Neither is strictly better — it's a different point on the risk/return spectrum, and which one makes sense depends entirely on whether they're trying to grow capital or protect income.
commonMistakes: Assuming preferred stock always pays a higher dividend than common stock
Forgetting that preferred shareholders typically have no vote
Treating preferred stock as equivalent to a bond rather than as its own distinct instrument
Overstating preferred's safety — it's still equity, and still subordinate to actual debt
keyPoints: Common stock: voting rights, residual profit claim, unlimited upside, lowest priority
Preferred stock: fixed dividend paid before common, priority in liquidation, no voting rights, limited upside
Preferred sits between common stock and bonds on the risk/return spectrum
The choice trades priority and stability against ownership and upside

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes voting rights between the two
Correctly describes the dividend and liquidation priority difference
Clearly frames the upside-vs-priority tradeoff

questions.title: A 'Crash' That Was Actually a Stock Split
questions.prompt: A junior colleague panics after seeing a stock's historical chart show a price that halves overnight with no news. What likely happened, and how should historical data actually be handled to avoid this confusion?
questions.modelAnswer: This is almost certainly a stock split — a 2-for-1 split doubles the share count and halves the price per share, leaving total market value unchanged, but a raw, unadjusted price series shows it as an overnight 50% drop with no corresponding news. The fix is to use adjusted prices: historical prices rescaled backward through time so that splits, dividends, and other corporate actions don't create artificial jumps. 'Adjusted close' is a standard column in essentially every historical price dataset for exactly this reason, and any analysis or backtest should default to using it rather than the raw close.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check, before assuming the data is wrong or the company had some disaster, is whether a corporate action lines up with that exact date — a split is the single most common explanation for a price series that jumps with zero news attached. I'd make it a habit, not a one-off check: always confirm you're working with adjusted close, because an unadjusted series will eventually produce exactly this kind of false alarm, or worse, quietly corrupt a return calculation without anyone noticing.
commonMistakes: Concluding the company had a real crisis without first checking for a corporate action
Using raw (unadjusted) close prices for return calculations by default
Assuming only dividends require price adjustment, forgetting splits and buybacks
Not verifying which adjustment convention a data vendor actually uses before trusting it
keyPoints: A stock split changes share count and per-share price without changing total market value
Unadjusted historical prices show splits (and dividends) as artificial price jumps
Adjusted close rescales historical prices so corporate actions don't distort the series
Always confirm which price column (raw vs. adjusted) a dataset or analysis is actually using

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies a stock split as the likely cause
Explains why the drop is not a real change in value
Recommends adjusted prices as the fix

questions.title: Explaining an Inverted Yield Curve to a Client
questions.prompt: A non-technical client reads that the yield curve has 'inverted' and asks what that means and why people seem worried about it. How do you explain it clearly?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain that normally, lending money for longer pays a higher interest rate than lending for a short time, because the lender wants extra compensation for locking their money up longer. An inverted yield curve means that relationship has flipped — short-term bonds are paying more than long-term ones. That's unusual, and it tends to happen when the market expects the central bank to cut interest rates significantly in the future, which pulls expected long-term yields below today's short-term yields. Historically, an inverted curve has often preceded economic slowdowns, which is why it gets attention — though it's a signal about expectations, not a guarantee of what will actually happen.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep the mechanics simple and lead with the plain-English version: normally you get paid more for locking money up longer, and right now that's backwards, which usually means the market expects rates to fall significantly down the road. I'd be careful to frame it as a signal worth watching, not a prediction — curves have inverted before without a recession following immediately, and clients deserve that nuance rather than a scare headline repeated back to them.
commonMistakes: Describing the yield curve without explaining what 'normal' looks like first
Presenting an inverted curve as a guaranteed recession signal rather than a historical pattern
Using unexplained jargon like 'term structure' or 'duration' with a non-technical client
Failing to explain the underlying expectations mechanism (anticipated rate cuts)
keyPoints: Normal yield curve: longer maturities yield more than shorter ones
Inverted yield curve: shorter maturities yield more than longer ones
Inversion typically reflects expectations of future rate cuts
Historically associated with, but not a guarantee of, an economic slowdown

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the normal shape before describing the inversion
Correctly explains the expectations mechanism behind inversion
Communicates in plain, non-technical language
Avoids overstating inversion as a guaranteed recession predictor

questions.title: Pricing a Stock Index Future
questions.prompt: A stock index trades at a spot price of $4,500. The continuously-compounded risk-free rate is 5%, the index pays no dividends, and a futures contract on it expires in 3 months. What should the futures price be, and is the market in contango or backwardation?
questions.code: F = S * e^((r + c - y) * T)
questions.modelAnswer: With no storage cost (c=0) and no dividend yield (y=0), F = S * e^(r*T) = 4,500 * e^(0.05*0.25) = 4,500 * e^0.0125 = 4,500 * 1.01258 ≈ $4,556.60. Since the futures price ($4,556.60) sits above the spot price ($4,500), this is contango — the normal state for an asset with no yield or convenience benefit, where the futures price simply reflects the cost of financing the spot price forward to delivery at the risk-free rate.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd just plug straight into cost-of-carry: no storage, no dividend, so it collapses to the simplest version, spot times e^(rT). The number comes out above spot, and that's exactly what should happen whenever there's a financing cost and no offsetting yield — contango isn't a market view here, it's just arithmetic.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert the 3 months into T=0.25 years before using it in the exponent
Applying simple (1+r)^T compounding when the problem specifies continuous compounding
Concluding backwardation when the futures price is actually above spot
Including a dividend yield adjustment when the problem states the index pays no dividends
keyPoints: F = S * e^((r + c - y) * T) under continuous compounding
With no storage cost or yield, the formula reduces to F = S * e^(rT)
Futures price above spot = contango; below spot = backwardation
Contango is the normal state when financing cost dominates and there's no offsetting yield

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the futures price
Correctly identifies contango vs. backwardation
Correctly simplifies the formula given no storage cost or yield

questions.title: Computing a Forward FX Rate
questions.prompt: GBP/USD spot is 1.25. The USD interest rate is 4% and the GBP interest rate is 6%, for a 1-year forward. Compute the forward rate using covered interest rate parity, and state whether the pound trades at a forward premium or discount against the dollar.
questions.modelAnswer: Treating USD as domestic and GBP as foreign: Forward = 1.25 * (1.04 / 1.06) = 1.25 * 0.98113 ≈ 1.2264. The forward rate (1.2264) is below the spot rate (1.25), so the pound trades at a forward discount against the dollar. This makes sense under covered interest rate parity: GBP earns the higher interest rate (6% vs 4%), so to prevent a riskless arbitrage (borrow USD, convert to GBP, earn the higher rate, convert back via the forward), the pound must be priced to weaken against the dollar in forward terms by roughly that rate differential.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always anchor on one rule before doing the arithmetic: whichever currency earns the higher interest rate has to trade at a forward discount, otherwise there'd be a free lunch. Here GBP earns more, so I already expect the forward to come in below 1.25 before I even finish the calculation — getting that direction right first catches sign errors before they happen.
questions.example: Forward = 1.25 * (1.04/1.06) ≈ 1.2264, below spot → GBP at a forward discount, USD at a forward premium.
commonMistakes: Inverting the ratio and dividing the foreign rate by the domestic rate instead of the reverse
Concluding a forward premium when the higher-yielding currency should show a forward discount
Mixing up which currency is 'domestic' and which is 'foreign' in the formula
Forgetting this is covered (forward-locked) parity, not a forecast of where spot will actually end up
keyPoints: Forward = Spot * (1 + r_domestic) / (1 + r_foreign)
The higher-interest-rate currency trades at a forward discount
Covered interest rate parity is a no-arbitrage condition, not a forecast
Getting the direction right before computing catches most sign errors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the forward rate
Correctly identifies the forward discount on GBP
Explains the no-arbitrage reasoning behind the direction

questions.title: A Two-Step Binomial Call Price
questions.prompt: A stock trades at S=$50. Over each of two steps, it can move up by a factor of u=1.2 or down by d=0.85. The risk-free rate is 3% per step (continuously compounded). Price a call option with strike K=$50 using the two-step binomial tree.
questions.professionalAnswer: I work it mechanically in the same order every time: compute p once, compute every terminal payoff, then step back one layer at a time, discounting each step. The most common place to slip up is reusing the real-world probability instead of the risk-neutral one, or forgetting to discount at each step rather than only once at the end — I double-check both before trusting the final number.
commonMistakes: Using a real-world up-probability instead of the risk-neutral probability p
Discounting only once at the very end instead of once per step
Mixing up which terminal node corresponds to up-down vs down-up (they're the same price on a recombining tree)
Forgetting to take max(S-K, 0) rather than S-K directly at the terminal nodes
keyPoints: Risk-neutral probability p is computed once from u, d, and r, not estimated from real-world odds
Terminal payoffs use max(S-K,0) for a call at every ending node
Backward induction discounts and averages one layer at a time
The final node-zero value is the option's fair price today

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the risk-neutral probability p
Correctly computes all three terminal payoffs
Correctly performs backward induction through both layers
Arrives at a final price close to $5.98

questions.title: Black-Scholes Call Price From Scratch
questions.prompt: Price a European call with S=$60, K=$55, r=4%, sigma=30%, T=0.25 years using the Black-Scholes formula. Show d1, d2, and the final price.
questions.code:
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)*T] / (sigma*sqrt(T))
d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(T)
C = S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2)
questions.professionalAnswer: I compute d1 and d2 first and sanity-check the sign before plugging into N(.) — a positive d1 here makes sense since the call is in the money (S>K). From there it's mechanical: look up or compute each N(.) value, multiply through, and discount the strike term by e^(-rT). I always double-check that I discounted the strike, not the spot — that's the easiest place to drop a term under time pressure.
commonMistakes: Discounting the spot price instead of the strike price
Forgetting to subtract sigma*sqrt(T) when computing d2 from d1
Using the wrong sign convention when looking up N(d1) vs N(-d1)
Not converting the time to expiration into years before using it
keyPoints: d1 and d2 combine moneyness, rate, volatility, and time
C = S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2) for a European call
The strike, not the spot, gets discounted at the risk-free rate
A positive d1 for an in-the-money call is a reasonable sanity check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes d1
Correctly computes d2 from d1
Correctly applies the call pricing formula with discounting
Arrives at a price close to $6.85

questions.title: American vs European Exercise
questions.prompt: Why is an American option never worth less than the equivalent European option, and why can't you just use the Black-Scholes formula to price it?
questions.modelAnswer: An American option grants every right a European option does (exercise at expiration) plus the additional right to exercise at any time before expiration. Extra optionality is never worth less — in the worst case, the holder simply never exercises early and the American option behaves exactly like the European one, so its value can only be equal to or greater than the European price, never less. Black-Scholes assumes exercise is only possible at expiration (it's derived specifically for European-style payoffs), so it has no mechanism for evaluating whether early exercise is ever optimal. Pricing an American option instead requires a method like the binomial tree, which checks at every node whether immediate exercise beats continuing to hold, or a finite-difference/PDE method that handles the same early-exercise comparison numerically.
questions.professionalAnswer: The 'extra right can't make something worth less' logic is the one-sentence version I'd give first — American is European plus an option on top of an option, and an extra choice is never a disadvantage. Black-Scholes is a closed-form answer to a specific question that doesn't include that extra choice, so reaching for it on an American option isn't 'close enough,' it's answering the wrong question entirely — you need the tree's node-by-node exercise check instead.
commonMistakes: Assuming Black-Scholes is a reasonable approximation for American options
Thinking early exercise is always beneficial rather than only sometimes optimal
Not recognizing that most listed U.S. equity options are American-style
Failing to explain why the binomial tree, not a closed-form formula, is the natural tool here
keyPoints: American options include every right a European option has, plus optional early exercise
Extra optionality can only add value, never subtract it
Black-Scholes assumes exercise only at expiration and cannot evaluate early exercise
Binomial trees (or finite-difference methods) handle American options by comparing exercise vs. hold at every node

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why American value >= European value
Correctly explains why Black-Scholes can't handle early exercise
Names an appropriate alternative pricing method

questions.title: Cheapening a Hedge With a Knock-Out Barrier
questions.prompt: A client wants downside protection on a stock position but thinks a vanilla put is too expensive. How could a knock-out barrier put reduce the cost, and what is the client actually giving up in exchange?
questions.modelAnswer: A knock-out put is structured to cease to exist — pay nothing, regardless of where the stock ends up — if the underlying touches a specified barrier level before expiration. Because the option can become worthless in scenarios where a vanilla put would still pay off, it's priced cheaper than the equivalent vanilla put. The client is trading away protection in the specific scenario where the stock falls far enough to hit the barrier and then potentially recovers or falls further — exactly the deep-tail scenario a hedge is often bought for in the first place. The barrier put makes sense when the client wants cheaper protection against a bounded range of moderate declines and is willing to accept that protection disappears in a severe, barrier-breaching selloff.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be direct with the client: cheaper protection here isn't free lunch, it's a specific trade — you're giving up coverage in exactly the scenario a hedge usually matters most, a sharp enough move to hit the barrier. I'd make sure they understand that before recommending it, and I'd ask whether their real concern is a moderate pullback (where the barrier structure works fine) or a genuine crash (where it might knock out right when they need it most).
commonMistakes: Presenting a knock-out structure as strictly better because it's cheaper, without naming the tradeoff
Not clarifying that the option disappears entirely once the barrier is touched, regardless of what happens afterward
Confusing a knock-out with a knock-in structure
Assuming barrier options are always easy to price with a closed-form formula
keyPoints: A knock-out option ceases to exist (pays nothing) once the barrier is touched
Knock-out structures are cheaper than the equivalent vanilla option precisely because of this reduced coverage
The tradeoff is losing protection in exactly the severe-move scenario a hedge is often meant to cover
Suitability depends on whether the client's real fear is a moderate move or a severe crash

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a knock-out is cheaper than a vanilla put
Clearly states what coverage the client gives up
Frames the suitability question appropriately for the client

questions.title: SMB and HML in Plain English
questions.prompt: A colleague asks what SMB and HML actually represent in the Fama-French factor model, without reading the formula first. How would you explain each one and what it's trying to capture?
questions.modelAnswer: SMB ('Small Minus Big') is the historical return spread between small-cap stocks and large-cap stocks — it's capturing the empirical pattern that small companies have tended to outperform large companies beyond what market beta alone would predict, often called the size premium. HML ('High Minus Low') is the historical return spread between stocks with a high book-to-market ratio (cheap, 'value' stocks) and those with a low book-to-market ratio (expensive, 'growth' stocks) — capturing the value premium, the pattern that cheaper stocks have tended to outperform more expensive ones beyond their market beta. Both factors are built the same way: a long-short portfolio that isolates one specific characteristic's return pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the plainest possible framing: SMB is asking 'does being small pay off, on average, beyond what the market factor already explains,' and HML is asking the same question about being cheap relative to book value. Both are literally built as a long-short trade — long the group with the characteristic, short the group without it — which is a detail worth mentioning because it's exactly how you'd estimate either premium yourself from raw data.
commonMistakes: Describing SMB or HML as a single stock's characteristic rather than a long-short portfolio return
Mixing up which side of HML is 'value' and which is 'growth'
Treating the factors as guaranteed premiums rather than historical empirical patterns
Confusing SMB/HML with the market factor from CAPM
keyPoints: SMB = small-cap minus large-cap return spread (the size premium)
HML = high book-to-market (value) minus low book-to-market (growth) return spread
Both are constructed as long-short portfolios isolating one characteristic
Both exist because CAPM's single market factor doesn't explain these empirical return patterns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains SMB and the size premium
Correctly explains HML and the value premium
Notes both are long-short portfolio constructions

questions.title: Stress Test or VaR? Picking the Right Tool
questions.prompt: A risk manager wants to know two different things: 'what's our typical worst-case loss on a normal bad day' and 'what happens to our book if 2008 happened again starting tomorrow.' Which risk tool answers each question, and why wouldn't the other tool work as well?
questions.modelAnswer: The first question — a typical worst-case loss threshold on a normal bad day — is exactly what VaR is built to answer: a statistical loss threshold at a given confidence level and horizon, estimated from recent historical or modeled return patterns. The second question — what happens if a specific historical crisis repeated — is a job for historical scenario replay, a form of stress testing: it applies 2008's actual market moves (equity, credit, rates, volatility) to today's portfolio. VaR would be the wrong tool for the second question because it's built from statistically typical patterns and generally understates genuinely unusual, crisis-level moves; stress testing would be the wrong tool for the first question because it only answers 'what if this specific scenario happens,' not 'what's typical.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the risk manager these are two different questions with two different tools, and reaching for one to answer the other is a common mistake. VaR is good at 'what's normal-bad' because it's built from recent statistical patterns; it's bad at 'what's a real crisis' because crises are, by definition, outside that normal pattern. Stress testing is the other way around — it's purpose-built to replay a specific extreme scenario, but it doesn't tell you anything about how often a typical bad day happens.
commonMistakes: Trying to use VaR alone to answer a crisis 'what if' question
Assuming stress testing can substitute for a statistical, everyday risk threshold
Not recognizing that VaR is built from recent, typical data and therefore underestimates true tail events
Treating historical scenario replay as a forecast rather than a replay of a specific past event
keyPoints: VaR answers 'what's a typical worst-case loss at a given confidence level and horizon'
Historical scenario stress testing answers 'what would happen if a specific past crisis repeated'
VaR is built from normal statistical patterns and tends to understate genuine crisis-level moves
The two tools are complementary, not substitutes for each other

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches VaR to the first question
Correctly matches stress testing to the second question
Explains why each tool wouldn't fit the other question

questions.title: Market Risk, Credit Risk, or Liquidity Risk?
questions.prompt: Classify each of these losses as primarily market, credit, or liquidity risk, and explain your reasoning: (1) a bond's price falls because interest rates rose; (2) a counterparty to a derivatives trade fails to pay what it owes; (3) a fund has to sell a large position at a steep discount because the market for that asset is thin.
questions.modelAnswer: (1) Market risk — the loss comes directly from a market price/rate movement (rates up, bond price down), with no counterparty failure involved. (2) Credit risk — the loss comes from a counterparty failing to meet its obligation, which is precisely the definition of credit risk, regardless of what market prices did. (3) Market liquidity risk — the loss comes not from the asset's price moving on its own, but from the fund's own need to exit a position in a thin market, where the trade itself creates part of the loss by moving the price against the seller. All three risk types can coexist in the same crisis — a firm facing funding pressure, for instance, might be forced to sell into an illiquid market, compounding market and liquidity risk at once — but each of these three examples has one clearly dominant type.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through each one by asking the same question: who or what caused the loss? Rates moving is a market-driven cause — straightforward market risk. A counterparty not paying is a credit failure, full stop, regardless of what the market itself did. And a forced sale into a thin market is specifically a liquidity problem — the asset's own price may not have independently changed at all; it's the act of trying to sell size into it that creates the loss.
commonMistakes: Classifying the counterparty default as market risk because a derivative's price is involved
Confusing market liquidity risk with funding liquidity risk
Not recognizing that a forced sale's cost is distinct from the asset's independent price move
Assuming only one risk type can ever be present in a real-world loss event
keyPoints: Market risk: loss from movements in market prices or rates
Credit risk: loss from a counterparty failing to meet an obligation
Market liquidity risk: loss from being unable to exit a position without moving its price
Real crises often involve more than one risk type interacting at once

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly classifies the bond example as market risk
Correctly classifies the counterparty example as credit risk
Correctly classifies the forced-sale example as liquidity risk

questions.title: What the Liquidity Coverage Ratio Actually Requires
questions.prompt: A new analyst hears that a bank must comply with the 'Liquidity Coverage Ratio' and assumes it's about how much capital the bank holds. What does the LCR actually require, and how is that different from a capital requirement?
questions.modelAnswer: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) is a Basel III rule requiring banks to hold enough high-quality liquid assets to survive a 30-day acute stress scenario — it's specifically about having enough readily sellable, cash-like assets on hand to meet short-term obligations if funding suddenly dries up. That's different from a capital requirement, which measures how much of a bank's balance sheet is funded by equity (a buffer against losses) rather than debt, scaled by the riskiness of its assets. A bank can be well-capitalized (solvent on paper) and still fail from a liquidity crunch if it can't convert assets to cash fast enough to meet obligations — which is exactly the funding liquidity risk the LCR is designed to guard against.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the mix-up directly: capital is about solvency — does the bank have enough of a cushion to absorb losses — while the LCR is about liquidity — does the bank have enough readily available cash-like assets to survive a short, sharp funding squeeze. They're both post-2008 safeguards, but they're answering completely different questions, and a bank can fail from a liquidity problem even while technically solvent on a capital basis.
commonMistakes: Confusing the LCR with a capital adequacy requirement
Thinking the LCR is about general profitability rather than short-term liquid-asset coverage
Not naming the specific 30-day stress horizon the LCR is built around
Assuming solvency and liquidity are the same thing
keyPoints: LCR requires enough high-quality liquid assets to survive a 30-day acute stress scenario
Capital requirements measure equity funding relative to risk-weighted assets, a solvency measure
A bank can be solvent (well-capitalized) and still fail from a liquidity crunch
Both are Basel III tools, but they address different risk types

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what the LCR actually requires
Correctly distinguishes liquidity from capital/solvency
Explains why a solvent bank can still fail from illiquidity

questions.title: Explaining Hedge Fund Strategies to a Friend
questions.prompt: A friend considering a career switch asks you to explain, in plain terms, the difference between a long/short equity fund, a global macro fund, and a market-making firm. How would you break it down?
questions.modelAnswer: A long/short equity fund picks individual stocks it thinks will rise and others it thinks will fall, often trying to reduce exposure to the overall market's direction so the bet is really about which stocks outperform which, not whether the market goes up or down. A global macro fund instead takes positions on big-picture economic views — currencies, interest rates, commodities — often across many countries, betting on things like a central bank's next move or a currency's direction. A market-making firm isn't trying to predict direction at all — it profits by continuously quoting both a buy and sell price and capturing the small spread between them, over and over, managing the risk of ending up with unwanted inventory rather than betting on where any one asset is headed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame the difference around what each firm is actually betting on: long/short equity bets on which individual companies outperform their peers, macro bets on big economic and policy trends, and market making barely bets on direction at all — it's closer to running a toll booth than making a prediction. That one framing usually clicks faster than listing definitions.
commonMistakes: Describing all hedge fund strategies as fundamentally the same (just 'picking stocks')
Assuming market making involves taking a directional view like the other two
Not distinguishing buy-side hedge funds from sell-side bank trading desks
Overpromising what any one strategy type guarantees in terms of returns
keyPoints: Long/short equity: bets on relative performance between individual stocks, often market-neutral
Global macro: bets on big-picture economic and policy trends across currencies, rates, and commodities
Market making: profits from the bid-ask spread repeatedly, not from directional prediction
Each strategy type has a genuinely different risk profile and skill set

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains long/short equity
Correctly explains global macro
Correctly explains market making as non-directional
Delivers the explanation clearly for a non-expert

questions.title: Explaining '2 and 20' Without Overpromising
questions.prompt: A candidate interviewing for a hedge fund analyst role asks you to explain the '2 and 20' fee model and what it means for their own compensation. How do you explain the structure honestly without implying a guaranteed payday?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain that '2 and 20' describes how the fund charges its investors, not what any individual employee is guaranteed to earn: a 2% annual management fee on assets under management, covering operating costs regardless of performance, plus a 20% performance fee on profits generated above some benchmark or high-water mark. That structure matters for compensation because in a strong year, the fund keeps a meaningful share of the profits it generates through the performance fee, and some of that can flow through to the people who generated it — but it's a structural fact about the business model, not a promise about any individual's bonus, which still depends on the firm, the year, the role, and individual performance.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be upfront that this explains the fund's revenue model, not a paycheck formula — I'd never want a candidate walking away thinking '2 and 20' translates into a specific number for them. I'd describe the mechanics plainly, then immediately pivot to: how that revenue actually gets split internally varies enormously by firm and role, and that's a conversation for the specific offer, not a general rule.

Describing 2 and 20 as a compensation plan rather than an investor fee structure
Failing to mention the high-water mark concept
Overpromising what a strong fund year means for an individual employee's pay

20% performance fee on profits above a benchmark or high-water mark
This describes the fund's revenue model, not a guaranteed individual payout
Actual individual compensation depends on firm, role, year, and individual performance

questions.title: Flattening Delta Doesn't Mean Risk-Free
questions.prompt: A junior teammate flattens an options book's delta and declares the portfolio 'hedged.' What risks are still sitting in that book, and why doesn't a delta-hedge address them?
questions.modelAnswer: Flattening delta only neutralizes the portfolio's first-order sensitivity to a small move in the underlying's price — it does nothing about gamma or vega. Gamma exposure means the portfolio's delta itself will drift as the underlying moves, since the options' deltas change with price while a stock hedge's delta stays fixed at 1 per share — so the 'hedged' position won't stay hedged once the price actually moves, and needs to be rebalanced. Vega exposure means the portfolio still has a real view on implied volatility: if volatility rises or falls with the stock price unchanged, the position's value changes anyway, and nothing in a stock-based delta hedge touches this at all, since a share of stock has zero vega.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the teammate: you've addressed exactly one risk, and there are at least two more sitting right there in gamma and vega. A delta-hedge is a snapshot, not a seal — the moment the stock moves, gamma means that snapshot is already out of date, and vega means you're carrying a volatility bet the whole time regardless of what the stock does. 'Hedged' needs a qualifier: hedged against what, and for how long.
commonMistakes: Declaring a position fully hedged once delta is flat, without checking gamma or vega
Assuming a stock-based hedge can offset volatility exposure
Not recognizing that a delta-hedge needs ongoing rebalancing, not a one-time trade
Confusing 'market-neutral in direction' with 'risk-free'
keyPoints: A delta-hedge only neutralizes first-order sensitivity to the underlying's price
Gamma exposure means the hedge drifts out of balance as the price moves
Vega exposure means the position still has a real view on implied volatility
A stock hedge has zero vega and cannot offset volatility risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies gamma exposure as remaining risk
Correctly identifies vega exposure as remaining risk

questions.title: Log Returns or Simple Returns?
questions.prompt: You need to compute (1) a portfolio's return today given its three holdings' individual returns, and (2) the cumulative return of one stock over 250 trading days. Which return type — simple or log — is the natural fit for each task, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: For computing today's portfolio return from three holdings' individual returns, simple returns are the right tool: they're cross-sectionally additive, meaning the portfolio's return is just the weighted average of the holdings' simple returns at that one point in time. For computing one stock's cumulative return across 250 days, log returns are the better tool: they're time-additive, meaning the cumulative log return is simply the sum of all the one-period log returns, turning a messy multiplicative compounding problem into simple addition. Using the wrong one for either task still works with extra steps (you can always convert), but each is specifically designed to make its respective task simpler and less error-prone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as: simple returns add up well across assets at one moment, log returns add up well across time for one asset. So weighting three holdings into a single day's portfolio return calls for simple returns, and building up 250 days of one stock's return calls for log returns. Mixing them up isn't fatal, but it makes the math needlessly awkward and is an easy place to introduce a silent error.
commonMistakes: Using log returns to compute a portfolio's weighted-average return across holdings
Summing simple returns across time instead of compounding them multiplicatively
Assuming the two return types are interchangeable without any adjustment
Forgetting that log returns need to be exponentiated to recover a percentage cumulative return
keyPoints: Simple returns are cross-sectionally additive — right for combining returns across assets at one time
Log returns are time-additive — right for combining returns across time for one asset
Cumulative log returns are summed; cumulative simple returns are compounded multiplicatively
Choosing the matching return type avoids unnecessary calculation errors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns simple returns to the portfolio-aggregation task
Correctly assigns log returns to the cumulative-return-over-time task

questions.title: Explaining Fat Tails to a Skeptical Colleague
questions.prompt: A colleague who's comfortable with basic statistics insists that modeling stock returns as normally distributed is 'close enough.' How would you push back using the concept of fat tails, in terms they'd find convincing?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd point out that if daily stock returns were truly normally distributed, moves of 5 or more standard deviations would be almost impossibly rare — a once-every-few-thousand-years event. In reality, markets produce moves like that regularly; stock market history is full of single days a normal model says should essentially never happen. This is 'fat tails' — real return distributions have far more probability mass in their extreme tails than a normal distribution predicts. The practical consequence of ignoring this isn't academic: any risk model built on a normal assumption will systematically underestimate the chance and size of a real crisis, right when getting that number correct matters most.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't argue the point abstractly — I'd point to history. Ask them how many '5-sigma' days a normal model predicts over a few decades (essentially zero), and then point out how many the market has actually produced. That gap is the whole argument in one comparison, and it's a lot more persuasive than reciting kurtosis definitions.
commonMistakes: Arguing the point only with the word 'kurtosis' rather than a concrete, relatable example
Not connecting fat tails to a practical consequence (risk models underestimating real crisis risk)
Conceding too much ground by implying normal is fine for anything except extreme events
Failing to note that this is an extremely well-documented, decades-old empirical finding, not a fringe view
keyPoints: Fat tails: real return distributions have more extreme-move probability than a normal distribution predicts
Normal-model-predicted extreme moves (5+ standard deviations) happen far more often in reality
A model assuming normality will systematically underestimate real risk, especially tail risk
This is one of the most well-established stylized facts of financial returns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what fat tails means
Uses a concrete, convincing example or comparison
