questions.title: Backfill Bias in a Hedge Fund Database
questions.prompt: A dataset of hedge fund returns shows an impressively high average historical return across all listed funds. A colleague wants to use this average as a baseline expectation for the industry. What bias should you check for first, and why would it inflate this specific number?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a classic setup for backfill (instant history) bias: a fund typically only starts voluntarily reporting its performance to a commercial database once it already has a good track record, and then backfills its historical returns into the database retroactively. Funds with bad early performance often never start reporting at all, so they simply never enter the dataset. The result is that the average historical return across funds in the database is inflated, because the funds that get backfilled are disproportionately the ones that did well — the database silently excludes the funds that would have dragged the average down. Using that average as an industry baseline would overstate what a typical hedge fund investor actually experienced.
questions.professionalAnswer: Any time I see an unusually strong average return from a voluntary-reporting database like this, backfill bias is the first thing I check, before I even look at anything else. The giveaway is the voluntary nature of the reporting — nobody signs up to show off a bad track record, so the dataset is quietly tilted toward winners before you've run a single calculation.
commonMistakes: Confusing backfill bias with survivorship bias (related, but distinct mechanisms)
Assuming a hedge fund database is representative just because it's commercially available
Not checking whether fund inclusion was voluntary and retroactive
Using the inflated average as a baseline without any adjustment or caveat
keyPoints: Backfill bias: funds join a database only after already having a good track record, then backfill history
Funds with poor early performance often never enter the database at all
This inflates the database's average historical return
Distinct from, but related to, survivorship bias

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies backfill (instant history) bias
Explains the voluntary, retroactive reporting mechanism
Explains why this specifically inflates the average

questions.title: Historical Volatility vs Realized Volatility
questions.prompt: Two colleagues both say they computed 'today's volatility estimate' for the same stock, but got different numbers. One used daily closing prices over a rolling window; the other used 5-minute intraday returns. Why might these differ, and which is generally considered the more statistically efficient estimate?
questions.modelAnswer: The first colleague computed historical (rolling) volatility: the standard deviation of daily close-to-close returns over a trailing window, which weights every day in the window equally and uses only one observation per day. The second computed realized volatility: using many intraday returns within each day and summing their squares, which uses far more data points per day. Realized volatility is generally considered the more statistically efficient (less noisy) estimate specifically because it's built from many high-frequency observations rather than a single daily return, giving a sharper picture of that day's 'true' volatility. The two numbers can genuinely differ because they're built from different underlying data, not because either calculation is necessarily wrong.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them both numbers can be 'right' — they're just answering the question with different amounts of information. Historical volatility is the simpler, more commonly available estimate when you only have daily closes; realized volatility is the sharper estimate when you have intraday data, because it's averaging over many more observations per day instead of just one. If intraday data is available, I'd lean on the realized number as the more trustworthy one.
commonMistakes: Assuming the two estimates should always match exactly
Not recognizing that realized volatility requires higher-frequency (intraday) data
Treating historical (rolling) volatility as inherently wrong rather than simply less data-rich
Forgetting both estimates still need annualizing to be comparable
keyPoints: Historical (rolling) volatility uses daily close-to-close returns, one observation per day
Realized volatility uses many intraday returns per day, summed as squared returns
Realized volatility is generally more statistically efficient due to using more data points
Both are after-the-fact measurements, not forecasts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the historical (rolling) volatility calculation
Correctly explains the realized volatility calculation
Correctly identifies realized volatility as more statistically efficient and explains why

questions.title: What GARCH Is Actually Modeling
questions.prompt: A colleague who's heard of GARCH but never used it asks what problem it's actually solving, in plain terms. What would you tell them it does, without writing out the formula?
questions.modelAnswer: GARCH is modeling the fact that volatility isn't constant — it comes in clusters, where a turbulent period tends to be followed by more turbulence, and a calm period tends to be followed by more calm. Rather than treating tomorrow's volatility as a fixed, unchanging number, GARCH lets today's variance depend on both how big yesterday's price shock was and how high yesterday's variance already was, so it can capture the fact that a market getting jumpy tends to stay jumpy for a while, and a quiet market tends to stay quiet. The practical payoff is a volatility forecast that reacts to current conditions rather than assuming the future looks just like the long-run historical average.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe it without any equations at all: GARCH is just a formal way of saying 'volatility has momentum of its own.' A big move today makes a big move tomorrow more likely, and GARCH is the model that actually lets that pattern feed into a forecast, instead of assuming volatility is some flat, unchanging constant.
commonMistakes: Describing GARCH as a return-forecasting model rather than a volatility-forecasting model
Not connecting GARCH back to the volatility clustering stylized fact it's built to capture
Assuming GARCH predicts the direction of the next price move
Treating GARCH's forecast as a fixed, single number rather than something that evolves period to period
keyPoints: GARCH models volatility clustering: calm and turbulent periods tend to persist
Today's variance depends on yesterday's shock size and yesterday's variance
GARCH forecasts volatility, not the direction of returns
The forecast adapts to current conditions rather than assuming a fixed long-run average

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains volatility clustering as the motivating pattern
Correctly explains GARCH forecasts volatility, not return direction
Explains this in plain, non-technical language

questions.title: Designing a Simple Volatility-Targeting Rule
questions.prompt: A portfolio holds a fixed dollar amount in a single volatile asset. After a quiet period, the asset's volatility doubles. What would a volatility-targeting approach do differently than holding a fixed dollar position, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: A fixed dollar position leaves the position size unchanged regardless of volatility, which means the position's actual risk contribution grows automatically whenever volatility rises — the portfolio is taking on more real risk without anyone deciding that on purpose. A volatility-targeting approach instead sizes the position inversely to its forecast volatility, so that the position's risk contribution (not its dollar size) stays roughly constant over time. If volatility doubles, a volatility-targeting rule would cut the position size roughly in half, keeping the expected risk level steady even as the asset's own behavior becomes more volatile, rather than passively absorbing more risk just because the market got choppier.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame the difference as: a fixed dollar position lets the market decide how much risk you're taking, while volatility targeting keeps that decision in your own hands. If vol doubles and you do nothing, you're suddenly carrying twice the risk you signed up for with no decision behind it — vol targeting is the rule that notices that and cuts the position before it becomes a problem.
commonMistakes: Assuming a fixed dollar position automatically controls risk the same way across market conditions
Not recognizing that volatility targeting changes position size, not the signal or conviction level
Confusing volatility targeting with simply avoiding volatile assets altogether
Forgetting that the inverse-volatility sizing needs an actual volatility forecast as an input
keyPoints: A fixed dollar position's risk contribution rises automatically when volatility rises
Volatility targeting sizes positions inversely to forecast volatility
The goal is to hold the position's risk contribution roughly constant over time
This requires an actual volatility forecast, such as one from a GARCH model

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the problem with a fixed dollar position under rising volatility
Correctly explains the inverse-volatility sizing rule
Explains the goal of holding risk contribution roughly constant

questions.title: Computing Each Position's Contribution to Return
questions.prompt: A portfolio holds Stock A at 70% weight with a 2% return, and Stock B at 30% weight with a -5% return this period. What is each position's contribution to the portfolio's total return, and what is the total?
questions.code:
Contribution_i = weight_i * return_i
Portfolio return = sum(Contribution_i)
questions.modelAnswer: Stock A's contribution = 0.70 * 0.02 = 0.014 (1.4 percentage points). Stock B's contribution = 0.30 * (-0.05) = -0.015 (-1.5 percentage points). Total portfolio return = 0.014 + (-0.015) = -0.001, or -0.1%. Despite Stock A having a positive return, the portfolio as a whole is slightly negative because Stock B's larger negative return, even at a smaller weight, outweighs Stock A's smaller positive contribution.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always compute contribution as weight times return for each position first, before even thinking about the total — that's the step people skip when they just eyeball 'one went up, one went down' and guess the portfolio is roughly flat or positive. Here it actually comes out slightly negative, which wouldn't be obvious without doing the weighted calculation.
commonMistakes: Averaging the two returns directly instead of weighting them
Forgetting to carry the sign through on the negative-return position
Confusing a position's own return with its contribution to the portfolio
Not checking that the weights sum to 1 (or 100%) before computing contributions
keyPoints: Contribution to return = weight × that position's own return
Portfolio return = sum of all positions' contributions
A position with a smaller weight can still dominate if its return is large enough in magnitude
Contribution, not standalone return, determines a position's actual effect on the portfolio

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes Stock A's contribution
Correctly computes Stock B's contribution
Correctly sums to the total portfolio return of -0.1%

questions.title: Reading Max Drawdown Off an Equity Curve
questions.prompt: A strategy's equity curve rises to a peak of $1.20 (from a $1.00 starting value), then falls to $1.05 before recovering to a new high of $1.30. What is the maximum drawdown, and at what point in this sequence does it occur?
questions.modelAnswer: The running maximum just before the decline is $1.20 (the peak reached). The trough of the decline is $1.05. Drawdown at the trough = 1.05/1.20 - 1 = -0.125, or -12.5%. That -12.5% is the maximum drawdown for this sequence — it's measured from the highest point reached so far down to the lowest point reached afterward, before a new high is set. The subsequent recovery to $1.30 doesn't change this number; it just means the drawdown has since fully recovered.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always anchor on the running peak first, not the starting value — drawdown is always measured from the highest point reached so far, not from where the strategy began. Here that peak is $1.20, so the trough of $1.05 gives a 12.5% drawdown, and the eventual recovery to a new high of $1.30 doesn't change that number at all; it just confirms the drawdown eventually fully recovered.
questions.example: Running max before decline = $1.20. Trough = $1.05. Drawdown = 1.05/1.20 - 1 = -12.5%.
commonMistakes: Measuring the decline from the starting value ($1.00) instead of the running maximum ($1.20)
Reporting the drawdown as a dollar amount instead of a percentage
Assuming the recovery to a new high changes the historical maximum drawdown value
Forgetting that drawdown is always zero or negative, never positive
keyPoints: Drawdown is measured from the running maximum (high-water mark), not the starting value
Max drawdown is the single worst (most negative) drawdown value reached
A subsequent recovery to a new high doesn't erase a prior max drawdown figure
Drawdown values are always zero or negative

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the running max as $1.20, not $1.00
Correctly computes the drawdown as -12.5%
Correctly notes the recovery doesn't change the max drawdown figure

questions.title: Calmar Ratio vs Sharpe Ratio
questions.prompt: Two strategies have the same Sharpe ratio, but an allocator strongly prefers one of them after also looking at their Calmar ratios. What is the Calmar ratio actually measuring that the Sharpe ratio doesn't, and why might that matter more to an allocator?
questions.modelAnswer: The Sharpe ratio measures return relative to total volatility — it penalizes all variability equally, whether it comes from a single catastrophic drawdown or many small day-to-day wiggles. The Calmar ratio instead measures annualized return relative to maximum drawdown, which specifically isolates the single worst peak-to-trough decline the strategy experienced. Two strategies can have identical Sharpe ratios while having very different maximum drawdowns, if one strategy's volatility is spread evenly while the other's is concentrated into one brutal event. An allocator often cares more about 'how bad could my single worst stretch with this manager realistically be' than about overall day-to-day bumpiness, which is exactly the question Calmar answers and Sharpe doesn't.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the allocator: Sharpe treats all volatility as equally bad, but in practice, what actually gets a manager fired (or gets an allocator to pull capital) is usually one brutal drawdown, not years of mild bumpiness. Calmar is built specifically around that worst-case event, which is why two strategies with the same Sharpe can look very different once you ask the Calmar question instead.
commonMistakes: Assuming Sharpe and Calmar should generally agree with each other
Describing Calmar without naming maximum drawdown specifically as its risk measure
Not explaining why an allocator might weight worst-case drawdown more heavily than average volatility
Treating Calmar as strictly superior to Sharpe rather than answering a different question
keyPoints: Sharpe = return relative to total volatility; penalizes all variability equally
Calmar = annualized return relative to maximum drawdown; isolates the single worst decline
Two strategies can share a Sharpe ratio while having very different max drawdowns
Allocators often care specifically about worst-case drawdown, which Calmar directly addresses

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines the Calmar ratio
Correctly contrasts it with what Sharpe measures
Explains why an allocator might care more about Calmar in this context

questions.title: A Sharpe of 1.0 That Isn't Actually Significant
questions.prompt: A two-year backtest shows a Sharpe ratio of 1.0, which sounds solid by the usual rule of thumb. A statistician points out this could still be statistically indistinguishable from a Sharpe of zero. How is that possible, and what should you actually report alongside the 1.0?
questions.modelAnswer: A Sharpe ratio is itself an estimate, not a fact, and it has its own sampling uncertainty — just like any mean computed from a finite, noisy sample. Over a relatively short sample like two years of daily data, that uncertainty can be large enough that a 95% confidence interval around the 1.0 point estimate stretches from clearly negative to strongly positive, meaning the data genuinely cannot rule out that the true underlying Sharpe is actually zero or negative. The fix isn't to distrust the 1.0 number outright, but to report it with its standard error and confidence interval attached, rather than as a bare point estimate — a Sharpe of 1.0 from 2 years of data deserves very different confidence than the same number from 15 years.
questions.professionalAnswer: A bare Sharpe number without its uncertainty is close to meaningless to me — I want the confidence interval right next to it, every time. Two years is a short sample, and it's completely normal for a seemingly solid Sharpe to have a confidence interval that includes zero or even goes negative. That's not a reason to throw the number out; it's a reason to be honest about how much weight it can actually bear.
commonMistakes: Treating a Sharpe ratio as a fixed fact rather than an estimate with its own uncertainty
Assuming a 'solid' Sharpe rule of thumb applies regardless of sample length
Reporting a point estimate without any confidence interval or standard error
Not recognizing that a longer sample would tighten the confidence interval around the same point estimate
keyPoints: A Sharpe ratio is an estimate with its own sampling uncertainty, not a fixed fact
A short sample (e.g., two years) can produce a wide confidence interval that includes zero
The point estimate alone doesn't convey how much confidence is actually warranted
Always report a Sharpe ratio alongside its confidence interval or standard error

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains that a Sharpe ratio has its own sampling uncertainty
Explains why a short sample can produce a wide confidence interval
Recommends reporting the confidence interval alongside the point estimate

questions.title: What a Market-Knowledge Interview Round Tests
questions.prompt: You're preparing for a trading-desk interview and notice there's a separate 'market knowledge' round distinct from the math and statistics rounds. What is this round actually testing, and how should your preparation differ from studying for a stats question?
questions.modelAnswer: A market-knowledge round tests whether you understand real market mechanics well enough to reason about risk in real time — how orders actually get filled, what moves a spread, how a market maker actually makes money, and what happens to a position or a book when markets move fast. This is different from a math or stats round, which tests probabilistic or modeling reasoning in the abstract. Preparation should focus on mechanics and fast, accurate reasoning under light time pressure — knowing order types cold, being able to do quick P&L arithmetic (long/short, different instrument types) without hesitating, and being ready to reason through a concrete market scenario (like a sudden rate surprise) using real structural concepts rather than vague statements like 'markets would be volatile.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell a candidate: this round isn't testing whether you can derive a formula, it's testing whether you'd be useful to have next to you on a desk during a fast-moving day. That means knowing the mechanics cold and being fast and accurate with simple arithmetic under a bit of pressure — practice dozens of quick long/short P&L drills until the sign never trips you up, because speed and accuracy under pressure is the actual skill being graded, not the difficulty of the math itself.
commonMistakes: Preparing for this round the same way as a probability or stats round
Giving vague, generic answers to scenario questions instead of naming specific mechanisms
Not practicing fast mental P&L arithmetic until it's instinctive
Underestimating how much this round values real-time, structural reasoning over abstract modeling
keyPoints: Market-knowledge rounds test real-time intuition about market mechanics, not abstract modeling
Order types, spread mechanics, and market-maker economics should be known cold
Fast, accurate P&L arithmetic under light time pressure is a core tested skill
Scenario answers should reference specific mechanisms, not vague generalities

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what the round is actually testing
Correctly distinguishes it from a math/stats round
Describes concrete, appropriate preparation strategies

questions.title: Researching a Compensation Range Before Negotiating
questions.prompt: You've just received a verbal offer from a prop trading firm and want to negotiate, but you don't have a confident sense of what the role typically pays. What should you actually do before naming a number, and why is it risky to rely on just one source?
questions.modelAnswer: Before naming a number, build a researched range from at least two independent sources specific to this firm type, role, and city — general aggregated salary sites (read skeptically, since quant roles are less reliably represented there than standard tech roles), live postings for comparable roles at comparable firm types, and your own network, since alumni or people in similar roles are often more candid about structure than any aggregated site. Relying on just one source is risky because quant compensation varies enormously by firm type — a prop shop's heavily PnL-linked structure can look completely different from a bank desk's steadier, more standardized bands even at the same seniority level — so a single data point, especially from a different firm type or city, can anchor you on a number that doesn't actually apply to this specific offer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd never walk into a negotiation with just one number in my head from one website — I'd triangulate from at least two independent sources specific to this exact firm type and city, because prop shop pay and bank-desk pay can look nothing alike even at the same title. Averaging a prop-shop number with a bank number produces a meaningless middle, not a useful range — the research has to be specific to the actual offer in front of you.
commonMistakes: Relying on a single salary website's number without cross-checking it
Averaging compensation figures across very different firm types instead of treating them separately
Not accounting for city-specific or firm-type-specific pay differences
Naming a number before doing any research at all
keyPoints: Build a researched range from at least two independent sources before negotiating
Compensation varies significantly by firm type (bank, hedge fund, prop shop), not just seniority
General salary aggregator sites should be read skeptically for quant-specific roles
A range specific to firm type and city is more useful than an averaged, generic number

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends researching before naming a number
Names at least two appropriate independent research sources
Explains why firm-type variance makes a single source risky

questions.title: Turning a Market Idea Into an Actual Strategy
questions.prompt: Someone says, 'I think stocks that go up tend to keep going up for a while.' Why isn't that a trading strategy yet, and what five things need to be pinned down before it becomes one?
questions.modelAnswer: That statement is an idea, not a strategy, because nobody could actually run it — it doesn't specify enough for a computer (or even a disciplined human) to execute it without ambiguity. A real systematic strategy needs five components defined in advance: the universe (which instruments are eligible, defined without hindsight), the signal (the precise rule that decides whether an instrument looks attractive and in which direction), position sizing (how much capital or risk a signal gets), risk rules (stop-losses, exposure caps, correlation limits that prevent one bad bet from being catastrophic), and execution (how the signal actually becomes an order, including timing and realistic costs). Until all five are specified, you have a hunch, not something that can be backtested or run.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them: if you can't write it down precisely enough that a computer with no judgment could execute it, it's not a strategy yet, it's a feeling about markets. The five-part checklist — universe, signal, sizing, risk rules, execution — is exactly the test I'd apply before calling anything a strategy, because each gap in that list is a place where hindsight can quietly sneak back in later.
commonMistakes: Treating a directional belief about markets as already being a tradable strategy
Naming only the signal and forgetting sizing, risk rules, or execution
Defining the universe using hindsight (e.g., 'the stocks that did well')
Assuming a strategy only needs to specify what to buy, not how much or when to exit
keyPoints: An idea is not a strategy until it's specified precisely enough to be executed without human judgment
The five required components: universe, signal, sizing, risk rules, execution
The universe must be defined without hindsight
A backtest is simply running all five components against historical data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why the original statement is an idea, not a strategy
Correctly names all five required components
Notes the importance of defining the universe without hindsight

questions.title: Alpha, Beta, and Edge — the Basic Split
questions.prompt: A strategy shows a positive annualized alpha in its backtest. Why isn't that number, by itself, proof that the strategy has a real edge?
questions.modelAnswer: A strategy's returns decompose into beta (its sensitivity to a market benchmark — the part of the return you could have earned for free with an index) and alpha (what's left over after beta is accounted for). A positive measured alpha has three possible explanations: a real, persistent edge; a statistical fluke from a finite sample; or an artifact of fitting the rule to data already seen. Edge specifically refers to the structural or informational reason alpha should exist and keep existing going forward — processing information faster, bearing a genuinely compensated risk, or exploiting a persistent structural friction. 'The backtest went up' is not itself a source of edge; it's a result that a real edge, or simply luck, could equally have produced.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently: alpha is a measurement, edge is an explanation, and a single backtest number only ever gives you the measurement. Before I'd call it real, I want to be able to answer 'why would this keep working' with something structural — faster information, a risk premium, a friction nobody's bothered to fix — not just point back at the chart and say it went up.
commonMistakes: Treating a positive backtested alpha as proof of a real edge on its own
Not distinguishing alpha (the measurement) from edge (the explanation for why it should persist)
Assuming 'the backtest went up' counts as a legitimate source of edge
Forgetting that alpha could be a statistical fluke or an overfitting artifact rather than real
keyPoints: Beta = sensitivity to a market factor; alpha = return left over after removing beta
A positive alpha could reflect a real edge, sampling luck, or overfitting
Edge is the structural or informational reason alpha should persist going forward
'The backtest went up' is a result, not itself evidence of edge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines alpha and beta
Correctly explains the three possible explanations for a positive alpha
Correctly distinguishes edge from the alpha measurement itself

questions.title: Momentum, Mean Reversion, and Carry: Each One's Failure Mode
questions.prompt: For each of momentum, mean reversion, and carry strategies, name the specific way that family characteristically fails. Why can't you just pick 'the best' one and ignore the others?
questions.modelAnswer: Momentum's characteristic failure is the momentum crash — a sharp reversal, often around a market turning point, that can wipe out months of gains quickly, because the strategy is by construction fully invested in whatever has recently worked. Mean reversion's characteristic failure is a regime shift — when a 'temporary' deviation is actually the start of a real trend, the strategy keeps adding to a losing position exactly when it should be cutting it, since the rule is built to buy dips and sell rips. Carry's characteristic failure is a carry crash — the position is usually small and steady until a risk-off shock hits, at which point the trade unwinds all at once, often correlated across many carry trades simultaneously. You can't just pick the 'best' one because none is unconditionally better — each has a plausible story, a regime it needs, and a distinct way it blows up, and professional allocators often blend all three precisely because those failure modes don't usually get triggered by the same event.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame each family by its failure, not just its story, because the failure is what actually determines how you should size and risk-manage it. Momentum blows up fast and sharply at turns; mean reversion bleeds slowly when a dip turns into a real trend; carry looks calm for a long time and then unwinds violently all at once in a risk-off shock. Blending them isn't about finding the 'winner' — it's about not having all your eggs exposed to the same kind of bad day.
commonMistakes: Describing only how each strategy is supposed to work, without naming its failure mode
Assuming one strategy family is unconditionally superior to the others
Mixing up which family fails from a sharp reversal versus a slow bleed versus a correlated unwind
Not recognizing why blending uncorrelated failure modes is a deliberate risk-management choice
keyPoints: Momentum's failure mode: a sharp momentum crash at a market turning point
Mean reversion's failure mode: a persistent regime shift turning a 'dip' into a real trend
Carry's failure mode: a correlated carry crash during a risk-off shock
No family is unconditionally better; blending them diversifies against different failure triggers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly names momentum's failure mode
Correctly names mean reversion's failure mode
Correctly names carry's failure mode
Explains why blending strategies is a deliberate choice, not indecision

questions.title: Correlated, Not Cointegrated: A Pairs Trade Gone Wrong
questions.prompt: A junior analyst builds a pairs trade on two stocks that were 90% correlated over the past year, but the trade loses money steadily as the two prices drift apart and never come back together. What did the analyst most likely skip checking, and why does high correlation alone not justify the trade?
questions.modelAnswer: The analyst most likely skipped checking for cointegration — a stable, mean-reverting long-run relationship between the two series — and relied on correlation alone. Two prices can be highly correlated over a sample and still wander apart forever, for instance if both simply trended up together during a broad bull market without ever having a genuine structural link forcing them back together. A pairs trade specifically needs the spread between the two (after an appropriately estimated hedge ratio) to be stationary — tested with something like the Engle-Granger procedure — not just a high correlation coefficient. A high correlation with no actual cointegration is exactly the setup that produces a pairs trade that looks promising on paper and then simply never reverts.
questions.professionalAnswer: High correlation without checking for cointegration is one of the most common ways to build a pairs trade that looks great in a correlation matrix and then just doesn't work. I'd ask the analyst directly: did you test whether the spread itself is stationary, or did you stop at 'these two move together'? Those are different questions, and only the second one actually justifies betting that the relationship reverts.
commonMistakes: Treating a high correlation coefficient as sufficient justification for a pairs trade
Not testing whether the spread between the two series is actually stationary
Assuming any two assets that moved together in the past will keep doing so
Confusing correlation (co-movement) with cointegration (a stable long-run relationship)
keyPoints: Cointegration, not correlation, is what actually justifies a pairs trade
Two series can be highly correlated and still never revert to any stable relationship
The standard test checks whether the spread (after a hedge ratio) is stationary
A pairs trade without a cointegration check is a bet on a relationship that may not exist

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing cointegration check
Explains why high correlation alone doesn't justify the trade
Mentions testing the spread for stationarity as the correct approach

questions.title: Writing a Falsifiable Hypothesis Before Touching the Data
questions.prompt: Why is 'momentum works' not a usable hypothesis for a backtest, and what specific pieces need to be pinned down to turn it into one that could actually fail?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Momentum works' is not falsifiable — it's vague enough that almost any result could be waved in to confirm it. A usable hypothesis needs five things pinned down in advance: the universe and period (exactly which instruments and which historical window, including a holdout reserved for later), the exact signal definition with no free parameters left to tune after seeing results, the expected direction and rough magnitude of the effect, a single success metric chosen before looking at any output, and kill criteria — the specific result that would make you discard the idea rather than keep tweaking it. Writing this down before touching the data matters because it's the only honest record of what you actually believed going in, since it's extremely easy to rationalize after the fact why a particular parameter 'obviously' made sense once you've already seen a favorable result.
questions.professionalAnswer: I treat an untestable idea like 'momentum works' as a red flag, not a starting point — if I can't say in advance what result would prove it wrong, I haven't actually designed a test yet. Writing the five pieces down before I touch the data is less about bureaucracy and more about defending myself from my own hindsight, because it's shockingly easy to convince yourself after seeing a good number that you knew it all along.
commonMistakes: Treating a vague directional belief as already being a testable hypothesis
Leaving signal parameters free to be tuned after seeing backtest results
Skipping a predefined kill criterion, making it easy to rationalize a disappointing result away
Not reserving a genuine holdout period untouched until final testing
keyPoints: A hypothesis must be falsifiable — specific enough that a result could prove it wrong
Five things to pin down in advance: universe/period, exact signal, expected direction/magnitude, success metric, kill criteria
Writing it down before seeing data defends against after-the-fact rationalization
This discipline is the first, cheapest defense against overfitting

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why the vague statement isn't falsifiable
Correctly names the five components to pin down
Explains why writing it down beforehand matters

questions.title: A Signal With Lookahead Baked Into a Misplaced Shift
questions.prompt: A backtest computes a momentum signal using each day's closing price, then assumes the position based on that signal could be entered at that same day's close. What's wrong with this, and what's the one-line fix?
questions.modelAnswer: This bakes in lookahead bias: the signal uses today's closing price, but a trader standing at the start of today couldn't possibly have known today's close yet — it hasn't happened. Assuming the position is entered at the same close the signal was computed from silently assumes perfect knowledge of the future, even though it looks like an innocent one-line piece of code. The fix is mechanical: shift the finished signal forward by at least one bar before it's allowed to generate a position, so a position decided from today's close can only be acted on starting tomorrow (or later), not today.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the single most common bug I'd check for first in any backtest — using today's close to decide and also trade on today's close. It looks completely harmless in the code, which is exactly why it's dangerous. The fix is one line: shift the signal forward by a bar before it touches position logic, and make that shift a habit you apply automatically, not something you remember to add only when you think to check.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing that this is a lookahead bias problem because the code 'looks fine' at a glance
Assuming a one-bar shift is unnecessary if the signal and trade happen 'close enough' in time
Fixing the shift for the signal but forgetting to check the execution/fill logic for the same issue
Treating this as a minor detail rather than one of the most common real backtest bugs

questions.title: Equal Weight, Signal Weight, or Inverse-Volatility?
questions.prompt: You have a signal ranking 50 stocks by attractiveness, and want to build a long-short portfolio from the top and bottom deciles. Compare equal weighting, signal weighting, and inverse-volatility weighting as construction choices, and explain when you'd lean toward each.
questions.modelAnswer: Equal weighting splits capital evenly across the selected names, ignoring how strong each one's signal value is — simple and robust, but it treats a barely-qualifying name the same as the most convicted one. Signal weighting instead scales each position by the strength of its own signal value, so the most convicted names get the most capital — this can improve returns if signal strength is genuinely informative, but it also concentrates risk into whichever names have the most extreme (and possibly noisiest) signal values. Inverse-volatility weighting sizes positions so each contributes roughly equal risk rather than equal capital, preventing a single volatile name from dominating the portfolio's actual risk regardless of its signal strength. The right choice depends on what you trust most: equal weight is the safest default when signal strength itself is uncertain, signal weighting makes sense when conviction genuinely varies and is reliably measured, and inverse-volatility weighting is the right tool specifically when controlling risk concentration matters more than following the signal exactly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default to equal weight unless I have a specific reason not to — it's the hardest to accidentally overfit. I'd only move to signal weighting if I had real confidence the signal's magnitude, not just its rank, carries information. And I'd reach for inverse-volatility weighting the moment I noticed one volatile name was quietly dominating the portfolio's actual risk despite looking like 'just one position' in dollar terms.

Not recognizing that signal weighting can concentrate risk into noisy extreme signal values
Confusing inverse-volatility weighting with weighting by signal strength
Picking a construction method without considering how it changes the portfolio's risk profile independent of the signal

Signal weighting: scales by conviction, but can concentrate risk into extreme (possibly noisy) signal values
Inverse-volatility weighting: sizes for roughly equal risk contribution, regardless of signal strength
The right choice depends on confidence in the signal's magnitude and how much risk concentration matters

questions.title: Sizing a Bet With the Discrete Kelly Formula
questions.prompt: A bet pays even money (b=1) and you believe you'll win it 58% of the time. What fraction of capital does the Kelly criterion say to risk, and what does it mean if that fraction comes out negative for a different bet?
questions.modelAnswer: With p=0.58, q=1-0.58=0.42, and b=1: f* = (1*0.58 - 0.42) / 1 = 0.16, or 16% of capital. If a different bet's calculation produced a negative f*, that means the bet has negative expected value at those odds, and Kelly is correctly telling you to take no position at all (or, if shorting is available, to bet the other way) — a negative Kelly fraction is not an instruction to bet a negative amount, it's a signal the bet itself isn't worth taking as structured.
questions.professionalAnswer: I compute it directly from the formula and sanity-check the sign before trusting it: a positive f* tells you how much edge-adjusted capital to risk, and a negative f* is Kelly's way of saying 'don't take this bet,' not a literal negative position size. Here, a 58% win probability at even odds gives a healthy-sounding 16% — though in practice I'd still scale that down with fractional Kelly before actually sizing a real position.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to compute q as 1-p before plugging into the formula
Interpreting a negative f* as an instruction to bet a negative size rather than to not bet at all
Treating full Kelly as the actual recommended position size without considering fractional Kelly
Mixing up b (payout odds) with p (win probability) in the formula
keyPoints: f* = (b*p - q) / b gives the Kelly fraction for a simple win/lose bet
A positive f* at even odds with a 58% win rate works out to 16% of capital
A negative f* means the bet has negative expected value — take no position
Full Kelly is rarely used as-is; fractional Kelly scales it down in practice

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes f* = 16%
Correctly interprets a negative f* as 'don't take the bet,' not a negative size

questions.title: Gross Exposure vs Net Exposure
questions.prompt: A long-short book holds $100M long and $100M short against $100M of equity. What is its gross exposure, what is its net exposure, and why does a risk manager care about both numbers separately?
questions.modelAnswer: Gross exposure is the sum of the absolute value of all positions: $100M long + $100M short = $200M, or 2x the $100M equity base (200% gross). Net exposure is the sum with sign: $100M long - $100M short = $0, or 0% net. A risk manager cares about both separately because they answer different questions: net exposure tells you how exposed the book is to the overall market's direction (here, close to none), while gross exposure tells you how much is actually at risk from financing costs, margin requirements, and what could go wrong if the correlation between the longs and shorts breaks down — a book can be perfectly net-neutral and still carry substantial risk and leverage through its gross exposure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd never let 'net exposure is zero' be the end of the risk conversation — gross exposure is the number that tells you how much leverage and correlation risk is actually sitting in the book. A book can look perfectly market-neutral on a net basis while running 200% gross, which means plenty can still go wrong if the long and short legs stop moving together the way they're supposed to.
commonMistakes: Computing gross exposure by netting long and short instead of summing their absolute values
Assuming a net-neutral book has no meaningful risk because net exposure is zero
Confusing gross exposure with leverage ratio without relating it back to equity
Not recognizing that gross exposure relates directly to financing and margin requirements
keyPoints: Gross exposure = sum of absolute value of all positions (long + short)
Net exposure = sum of signed positions (long minus short)
Net exposure measures exposure to overall market direction
Gross exposure measures financing, margin, and correlation-breakdown risk, independent of net

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes gross exposure as $200M / 200%
Correctly computes net exposure as $0 / 0%

questions.title: Telling a PM a Backtested Edge May Not Scale
questions.prompt: A portfolio manager is excited about a strategy's backtested Sharpe ratio and wants to allocate $200 million to it. The backtest was run at an illustrative $500,000 position size. How do you raise the capacity question without sounding like you're dismissing the research?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd frame it as a natural next question rather than a objection to the research itself: a backtest run at a small, illustrative size never sees market impact, because a small order doesn't move the price — so a strategy's Sharpe ratio at $500,000 of capital tells us very little about what the same strategy would achieve at $200 million, where our own trading would start consuming a meaningful share of daily volume and pushing prices against us. I'd propose running the numbers through a market impact model (such as the square-root model, where cost grows with the square root of the fraction of average daily volume traded) to estimate the capital level at which costs would erode the edge, and present that as the strategy's approximate capacity ceiling before committing the full allocation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lead with genuine enthusiasm for the research, then pivot to: 'the one thing the backtest hasn't tested yet is us' — our own footprint at $200 million wasn't part of that $500,000 test. I'd ask for the chance to run a capacity estimate before the full allocation goes out, framed as protecting the strategy's good result, not undermining it.
commonMistakes: Raising the capacity concern in a way that sounds dismissive of good research
Assuming a strategy's backtested Sharpe ratio is size-independent
Not proposing a concrete next step (a capacity estimate) alongside the concern
Waiting until after the full allocation to raise the issue
keyPoints: A backtest run at a small size never reveals the strategy's own market impact
Market impact cost rises with the square root of the fraction of average daily volume traded
Capacity is the capital level at which modeled impact cost erodes the gross edge to near zero
Raise this as a natural next research step, not as a dismissal of the existing result

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why a small-size backtest doesn't reveal market impact
Proposes a concrete capacity-estimation next step
Delivers the point constructively, without dismissing the research
